Behaviour Suite for Reinforcement Learning

bsuite trades a single leaderboard score for 23 named diagnostic experiments across seven RL capabilities -- basic competence, noise, scale, exploration, credit assignment, memory, generalization -- each reduced to a [0,1] score and reported as a capability radar, not a rank.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By 2019, RL benchmarks had mostly moved in one direction: toward more complexity. The Arcade Learning Environment turned dozens of Atari 2600 games into a shared testbed for deep RL (Bellemare et al., 2013); continuous-control suites (Duan et al., 2016; Tassa et al., 2018), model-based-RL benchmarks (Wang et al., 2019), and rich 3D environments like DeepMind Lab (Beattie et al., 2016) followed the same pattern -- together, the paper describes them as "natural successors to 'CartPole' or 'MountainCar'" that fold many core agent capabilities together into one integrated task. That's good for showing an agent can do something impressive end-to-end, but it makes it hard to answer a narrower, more useful question: why did an agent fail, or succeed? A high Atari score doesn't tell you whether an agent has good memory, good exploration, or neither -- it tells you it's good at Atari.

Meanwhile, the RL theory literature has its own targeted "unit test" environments -- RiverSwim for exploration (Strehl & Littman, 2008), Taxi for temporal abstraction (Dietterich, 2000) -- but the paper argues these are typically fixed-size, one-off constructions without a shared methodology for running or scoring an arbitrary agent against them, "something that has become a major problem for many benchmark suites" (citing Machado et al., 2017, on ALE's own evaluation-protocol drift). The paper frames its goal explicitly as complementary to both traditions: not a bigger integrated challenge, and not one more bespoke diagnostic script, but a shared, versioned, "MNIST for RL" -- a library of targeted experiments, each isolating one capability, that runs the same way and reports the same kind of score for any agent you plug in.

// how it works

The method

A bsuite experiment has three parts: a set of environments determined by some parameter (typically a size N), a fixed interaction protocol (e.g. a number of episodes), and an analysis that reduces the agent's logged behaviour to a single summary "score" in [0,1] -- "quick and dirty," in the paper's words, but standardized across agents and codebases. The paper requires every experiment (current or future) to be targeted (maps to one key RL issue), simple (strips away confounds), challenging (pushes agents past the normal range), scalable (reveals a scaling trend, not just pass/fail), and fast (under 30 minutes on a standard CPU) -- and states that bsuite "aims to remove all confounds from the core agent capabilities of interest," in contrast to benchmarks that add complexity.

The bsuite2019 release documented in Appendix A specifies 13 named environment designs: 5 "basic" tasks (a finite-armed bandit, an MNIST contextual bandit, Catch, Cartpole, and Mountain Car -- each run with 20 seeds and scored as normalized regret against random/optimal), 3 exploration tasks (deep sea, stochastic deep sea, cartpole swingup), 3 credit-assignment tasks (umbrella length, umbrella features, discounting chain), and 2 memory tasks (memory length, memory bits). The 5 basic tasks are each rerun a second and third time -- their 20 seeds split across 5 Gaussian noise levels (σ = 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10; 4 seeds each) and, separately, across 5 reward-scaling levels (λ = 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100; 4 seeds each) -- which is how the release's actual output, the per-experiment bar chart in Figures 6/7, ends up with 23 distinctly-named bars (5 basic + 5 noise + 5 scale + 3 exploration + 3 credit-assignment + 2 memory), rolled up into the 7 capability categories on the radar plot: Basic, Generalization, Noise, Scale, Exploration, Credit Assignment, Memory.

The paper walks through two experiments as worked examples. Deep sea is an N×N grid where the agent starts top-left and descends one row per step, with a fixed but randomized left/right mapping in every cell; moving right costs r = -0.01/N every step but pays +1 if the agent moves right at every step of the episode -- so a purely random policy reaches the reward with probability 2-N, and the small per-step cost actively pulls a greedy agent away from the one path that pays off. The main text runs this at sizes N = 10, 12, .., 50 for 10k episodes and scores the percentage of seeds whose average regret drops below 0.9 faster than the 2N episodes dithering would need.

Memory length is a stylized T-maze parameterized by length N: the agent observes a binary context bit only at step 1 (all later steps show 0), and must reproduce that bit as its action at step N to earn ±1 reward; the paper sweeps N = 1..100 (log-spaced) for 10k episodes and scores the percentage of seeds whose average regret over the run stays under 75% of what a uniformly random policy would get.

To demonstrate the suite, the paper runs three baseline agents from bsuite/baselines against it: DQN (Mnih et al., 2015), A2C (an actor-critic with a recurrent network, labeled actor_critic_rnn in the plots; Mnih et al., 2016), and Bootstrapped DQN with prior networks (Osband et al., 2016; 2018) -- plus a uniform-random agent as a sanity floor. Two further appendices (D, E) reuse the same suite as a diagnostic tool on a single algorithm family: comparing SGD, RMSProp, and Adam as DQN's optimizer, and comparing ensemble sizes {1, 3, 10, 30} for Bootstrapped DQN. The paper is explicit that these three reports are worked examples of how to use bsuite, not an exhaustive baseline study -- "we provide examples of specific investigations using bsuite in Appendixes C, D and E," each framed around illustrating a research workflow rather than establishing a definitive leaderboard.

// what they found

The results

On memory length (Figure 2), the recurrent actor-critic "greatly outperforms the feedforward DQN and Bootstrapped DQN," both of which "are unable to learn anything for length > 1, they lack functioning memory." But the recurrent agent's advantage has a sharp, explainable edge: it "performs well for all N ≤ 30 and essentially random for all N > 30, with quite a sharp cutoff," which the paper attributes directly to the fact that "the RNN agent was trained via backprop-through-time with length 30" -- the summary score recovers exactly the scaling limit the training procedure implies.

On deep sea (Figure 4), the pattern flips: "only Bootstrapped DQN, which was developed for efficient exploration, scores well," while DQN and the recurrent actor-critic both fail to solve any tested size up to N = 50 within the 10k-episode budget. Bootstrapped DQN's episodes-to-solve rise "gracefully" with N and stay far below the dashed 2N random-dithering reference curve the paper plots for comparison, leading the authors to suggest (without testing it) that the algorithm "might" continue scaling past N = 50.

The full-suite comparison (Appendix C, Figures 6/7) rolls all 23 experiments up into the 7-axis radar and a per-experiment bar chart, run for four agents: random, DQN, Bootstrapped DQN, and actor-critic-RNN. The paper's own commentary: "random performs uniformly poorly, confirming the scores are working as intended"; "dqn performs well on basic tasks, and quite well on credit assignment, generalization, noise and scale [but] extremely poorly across memory and exploration tasks [since] the feedforward MLP has no mechanism for memory, and ϵ=5%-greedy action selection is inefficient exploration"; "boot dqn is mostly identically to DQN, except for exploration where it greatly outperforms" [sic, as printed]; and "actor critic rnn typically performs worse than either DQN or Bootstrapped DQN on all tasks apart from memory. This agent is the only one able to perform better than random due to its recurrent network architecture."

The two follow-up appendices use the suite as a diagnostic tool for a single hyperparameter choice rather than an agent-vs-agent leaderboard. Appendix D reports that, for DQN's optimizer, "both RMSProp and Adam perform better than SGD in every category. In most categories, Adam slightly outperforms RMSprop, although this difference is much more minor. SGD performs particularly badly on environments that require generalization and/or scale." Appendix E reports that, for Bootstrapped DQN's ensemble size, "increasing the size of the ensemble improves bsuite performance across the board," but "we do see signficantly decreasing returns to ensemble size, so that ensemble 30 does not perform much better than size 10" [sic, as printed]; the gains are "most extreme in the exploration tasks, where ensemble sizes less than 10 are not able to solve large 'deep sea' tasks, but larger ensembles solve them reliably." Even at ensemble size 30, the paper notes its implementation "does not completely solve every cartpole swingup instance," which it speculates may reflect optimization instability rather than an exploration failure.

The paper reports the practical cost of running the full suite as well: "at August 2019 pricing, a full bsuite evaluation for our DQN implementation cost under $6" -- a specific, one-off number for one agent on one cloud setup, not a general claim about every agent's evaluation cost.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

bsuite is unusually candid about its own scope, and that candor is worth taking at face value: it states plainly that it is "not a replacement for 'grand challenge' undertakings in artificial intelligence, or a leaderboard to climb," that the authors "do not claim to capture all, or even most, of the important issues in RL," and even names a specific gap in the 2019 release -- "a notable omission from the bsuite2019 release is the lack of any targeted experiments for 'hierarchical reinforcement learning' (HRL)." Judged as what it says it is -- a shared, cheap, reproducible diagnostic library, not a ranking system -- the paper mostly delivers.

Two things are worth flagging precisely because the paper's own tables and figures disagree with each other in small but checkable ways. First, Appendix A's per-experiment tables list the "issues" tag for both memory experiments -- memory length (A.6.1) and memory bits (A.6.2) -- as "credit assignment," not "memory," even though Section A.6's own header and intro text describe them as testing memory, and Figures 6/7's bar-chart legend colors both memory_len and memory_size as the "memory" category (purple), not "credit_assignment" (red). The appendix table and the figure legend disagree about which category these two experiments belong to; nothing in the text resolves which is the intended ground truth. Second, the "deep sea" sweep is described two different ways in the same paper: the main text (§2.2) says "we run the agent on sizes N = 10, 12, .., 50," while Appendix A.4.1's table entry for the same experiment says "size N=[5..50]" -- a different lower bound and a coarser description of the step. Third, memory length's episode budget is likewise inconsistent: the main text runs it for 10k episodes while Appendix A.6.1's table entry gives the same experiment "1k episodes" -- a 10x difference, and the appendix additionally scores it as continuous "regret normalized [random, optimal] →[0,1]" rather than the main text's percentage-of-runs framing. None of these three is individually a large error, but all are small, checkable seams in a paper whose whole premise is precise, standardized measurement.

A more substantive limitation is statistical: the noise and scale variants of each basic task split 20 seeds across 5 conditions, i.e. 4 seeds per condition, and the paper reports no confidence interval, standard error, or seed-count sensitivity analysis anywhere for any of its scores -- not for the continuous regret-normalized scores, and not for the percentage-of-runs scores used by deep sea, stochastic deep sea, and cartpole swingup, none of which states how many runs each reported percentage is computed over. For a suite whose stated purpose is to "collect clear, informative and scalable problems," the absence of any uncertainty quantification around the one number every experiment produces is a real gap, not a stylistic one.

There is also a tension between the design goal and the actual specification: the paper states bsuite "aims to remove all confounds from the core agent capabilities of interest," yet several individual experiments carry two or three "issues" tags at once in Appendix A -- MNIST is tagged "basic, generalization"; Cartpole and Mountain Car are each tagged "basic, credit assignment, generalization"; stochastic deep sea is tagged "exploration, stochasticity"; both umbrella experiments are tagged "credit assignment, stochasticity." An experiment that is itself tagged with two or three capabilities is, by the paper's own bookkeeping, not fully isolating one -- which doesn't undermine the overall diagnostic approach, but does mean a single radar-plot axis can sometimes be a blend rather than a pure read of the capability it's named after.

Finally, the worked comparison in Appendix C uses only three baseline agents -- DQN (Mnih et al., 2015), the recurrent actor-critic A2C (Mnih et al., 2016), and Bootstrapped DQN with prior networks (Osband et al., 2016; 2018) -- plus a random floor; reasonable choices to illustrate the methodology, and the paper is explicit these are "examples," not a definitive baseline suite. But it's a narrow family: two feedforward DQN variants plus one recurrent actor-critic, all from a single lineage of value-based and actor-critic methods. The paper does not show whether a model-based, distributional, or policy-gradient-at-scale agent would still separate cleanly on the same axes, so the reader has to take the capability-isolation claim somewhat on faith for anything beyond this specific trio.

baselines

Three simple, explicitly-labeled-as-illustrative baseline agents from one narrow family (DQN, 2015; A2C/actor-critic-RNN, 2016; Bootstrapped DQN with prior networks, 2016/2018) -- two feedforward DQN variants plus one recurrent actor-critic; no model-based, distributional, or policy-gradient-at-scale agent is run against the full suite in this paper.

contamination

Not applicable in the training-data-leakage sense -- bsuite is a set of procedurally-defined RL environments, not a static dataset an agent could have memorized in advance.

what's missed

No confidence intervals anywhere, despite several scores resting on as few as 4 seeds per condition; a table/figure disagreement over whether the two memory experiments' "issue" tag is memory or credit assignment; a main-text/appendix disagreement on deep sea's exact size sweep; and an admitted gap (no HRL diagnostics).

would raise confidence

Reporting variance or a confidence interval around each summary score; reconciling the memory-experiment tag and the deep-sea sweep description between text and appendix; and running at least one more model-based, distributional, or policy-gradient-at-scale agent through the full 23-experiment suite to show the capability profile still separates cleanly beyond the three baselines shown here.

// bottom line

bsuite's real contribution is procedural: a cheap, shared, reproducible way to ask "why does my agent fail at X" instead of "how good is my agent overall" -- and the paper is unusually honest about that scope, including naming its own missing HRL diagnostics. But the demonstrated instantiation here -- three baselines from one narrow agent family, no uncertainty estimates on any score, and a few small text/table/figure disagreements about exactly what a given experiment is measuring -- is best read as a proof of concept for the methodology, not as evidence that every axis of the radar plot cleanly isolates the single capability it's labeled with.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. bsuite reframes RL evaluation as diagnosis rather than competition: 13 named environment designs, expanded into 23 named experiment instances once the 5 basic tasks are crossed with 5 noise levels and 5 reward-scaling levels, rolled up into 7 capability categories (basic, generalization, noise, scale, exploration, credit assignment, memory) and reported as a [0,1]-per-axis radar, not a single leaderboard number.
  2. The paper's own worked example is a clean, falsifiable story that a headline score alone can't tell: Bootstrapped DQN -- designed specifically for efficient exploration -- is the only one of three baselines to solve "deep sea" reliably and scale gracefully to N = 50, while the recurrent actor-critic is the only baseline to beat random on memory length, and only up to length 30, exactly matching its 30-step truncated backprop-through-time.
  3. bsuite is designed as a living, curated project rather than a fixed dataset -- DeepMind committed to an annual "bsuite committee" review at NeurIPS to add or replace experiments -- but the 2019/2020 release evaluated here shows real seams: no uncertainty quantification on any score, a few small internal disagreements between the main text, appendix tables, and figure legends about what a given experiment measures, and a demonstrated capability separation that so far rests on only three baseline agents from one narrow family.
